cards.front: In the nitrogen cycle, what is usable nitrogen?
cards.back: Nitrogen changed out of the gas into small particles that plants can take in, mostly from soil water.
cards.quote: nitrogen changed out of the gas into small particles that roots can take in, mostly from soil water

cards.front: The air is about 78 percent nitrogen, yet corn farmers in Virginia add nitrogen to their fields. Why does the air's nitrogen not feed the corn?
cards.back: Nitrogen gas must be changed into usable nitrogen before plants can use it. Where nitrogen runs short, what a field can grow depends on its usable nitrogen, not on the nitrogen in the air.
cards.quote: So what a field can grow depends on how much usable nitrogen it has, not on how much nitrogen is in the air.

cards.front: Why do living things need nitrogen?
cards.back: Every protein and all DNA contain nitrogen, so plants and animals need it to build them.
cards.quote: Living things need nitrogen for proteins and DNA, but nitrogen gas must be changed into usable nitrogen before plants can use it.
cards.section: Explain: what the lock is

cards.front: What is the "lock" that keeps nitrogen gas from being used, and why does it take so much energy to open?
cards.back: A particle of nitrogen gas is two nitrogen atoms stuck together very tightly. Pulling them apart takes a lot of energy.
cards.quote: A particle of nitrogen gas is two nitrogen atoms stuck together very tightly; that link is the lock.
cards.section: Explain: what the lock is

cards.front: Name the three things that change nitrogen gas into usable nitrogen.
cards.back: Bacteria, lightning and factories.
cards.quote: Bacteria, lightning and factories change nitrogen gas into usable nitrogen.
cards.section: Explain: never used up, but it can leave

cards.front: Bacteria in root nodules change nitrogen gas, which needs a large energy supply. Where do they get the energy?
cards.back: From food the plant makes from its sugar. Nodules are small bumps on the roots of beans, peas, soybeans and peanuts.
cards.quote: Those in root nodules, small bumps on the roots of beans, peas, soybeans and peanuts, get it as food the plant makes from its sugar.
cards.section: Explain: what the lock is

cards.front: {{c1::Animals}} get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
cards.quote: Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
cards.section: Explain: never used up, but it can leave

cards.front: The loop is the nitrogen cycle: the movement of nitrogen from the air, through the soil, into living things and back to the {{c1::air}}.
cards.quote: The loop is the nitrogen cycle: the movement of nitrogen from the air, through the soil, into living things and back to the air.
cards.section: Explain: never used up, but it can leave

cards.front: A dead deer lies in a Virginia forest. What happens to the nitrogen in its body?
cards.back: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead things (decomposers) return it to the soil as usable nitrogen, so plants can take it up again.
cards.why: Nitrogen atoms are never made or destroyed. They only change form.
cards.quote: Decomposers (fungi and bacteria that break down dead things and wastes) return it to the soil as usable nitrogen.
cards.section: Explain: never used up, but it can leave

cards.front: A flooded, soggy field has soil with very little oxygen. What happens to some of its usable nitrogen?
cards.back: Some soil bacteria change it back into nitrogen gas, which goes back into the air, so the field loses nitrogen.
cards.why: The cycle says this happens especially in soggy soil with little oxygen.
cards.quote: Other soil bacteria change some usable nitrogen back into nitrogen gas in the air, especially in soggy soil with little oxygen.
cards.section: Explain: never used up, but it can leave

cards.front: How does the nitrogen cycle connect to the carbon cycle?
cards.back: Plants use sugar from photosynthesis to build proteins with nitrogen, so the two cycles meet inside every leaf.
cards.quote: Plants use sugar from photosynthesis to build proteins with nitrogen, so the two cycles meet inside every leaf.
cards.section: Explain: never used up, but it can leave

cards.front: In a Michigan field, scientists grew two nearly identical soybean kinds side by side with no fertilizer. One kind could not form root nodules. What did this design let them test?
cards.back: Whether nodules help soybeans get nitrogen. Both kinds had the same air and soil, so the nodules were the main difference.
cards.quote: In Michigan, scientists grew two nearly identical kinds of soybean side by side in one field for three summers.
cards.section: Evidence: do the bumps open the gate?

cards.front: In the Michigan field in 2008, soybeans with nodules held 148 kg of nitrogen per hectare and soybeans with no nodules held 61.6 kg. How many more kilograms did the nodule plants hold?
cards.back: 148 - 61.6 = 86.4 kg per hectare more.
cards.why: The same subtraction in 2007 was 144 - 67.6 = 76.4 kg.
cards.quote: The difference is 144 − 67.6 = 76.4 kg. So the plants with nodules held about twice as much.
cards.section: Evidence: do the bumps open the gate?

cards.front: Soybeans with nodules held 282, 144 and 148 kg of nitrogen per hectare over three summers. Find the mean.
cards.quote: Find the mean (average) nitrogen over the three years for plants with nodules: add the three numbers and divide by 3.
cards.section: Evidence: do the bumps open the gate?

cards.front: The air above one hectare holds about 78,000 tonnes of nitrogen, yet nodule soybeans held only about 0.19 tonnes above ground. What does this show?
cards.back: A plant's growth depends on its usable nitrogen, not on the nitrogen gas in the air (where nitrogen is what runs short).
cards.quote: Yet the soybeans with nodules held on average only about 0.19 tonnes (191 kg) above the ground.
cards.section: Evidence: do the bumps open the gate?

cards.front: Soybeans with nodules held about twice the nitrogen on average over the three years of soybeans without nodules, and no fertilizer was added. What claim fits, and why is the bar difference not an exact measure of the bacteria's share?
cards.back: Claim: nodule bacteria likely supplied the extra nitrogen. But even nodule plants took some nitrogen from the soil, so the difference is not an exact measure.
cards.quote: Even the plants with nodules took some nitrogen from the soil, so the difference between the bars is not an exact measure of what the bacteria supplied.
cards.section: Evidence: do the bumps open the gate?

cards.front: A test tracking two natural forms of nitrogen atoms estimated how much of the nodule soybeans' nitrogen came from the air. Why was that higher than the simple difference between the bars?
cards.back: About 60 to 70 percent came from the air through the bacteria, an estimate, not an exact measure. It is higher because plants with nodules take less nitrogen from the soil than plants without them.
cards.quote: It is higher than the simple difference between the bars, because plants with nodules take less nitrogen from the soil than plants without them.
cards.section: How scientists estimated where the nitrogen came from

cards.front: You test whether root bacteria help pea plants in low-nitrogen soil. What is the independent variable, and what is the control?
cards.back: Independent variable: seeds coated with a garden inoculant (root-nodule bacteria) or not coated. Control: pots of uncoated seeds.
cards.quote: Independent variable: seeds coated with a garden inoculant (a powder of root-nodule bacteria sold for peas and beans) or not coated.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What happens in an ecosystem with too little usable nitrogen?
cards.back: Plants grow less, and deer and other animals have less food.
cards.quote: Many ecosystems (places and all the living things in them) have too little, so plants grow less and deer and other animals have less food.
cards.section: Explain: too little or too much nitrogen

cards.front: An algal bloom in the Chesapeake Bay dies and sinks. What could this do to fish and crabs near the bottom?
cards.back: Decomposers breaking down the dead algae use up oxygen that fish and crabs need.
cards.quote: Decomposers break down the dead algae, and as they do, they use up oxygen that fish and crabs need.
cards.section: Explain: too little or too much nitrogen

cards.front: When scientists added nutrients, including nitrogen, to grassland plots around the world, what happened to the plants?
cards.back: The plants grew thicker, but fewer kinds grew. So extra nutrients can lower biodiversity.
cards.quote: When scientists added nutrients, including nitrogen, to grassland plots around the world, the plants grew thicker, but fewer kinds grew.
cards.section: Explain: too little or too much nitrogen

cards.front: In nutrient-added grassland plots, thicker growth leaves less light near the ground. A fence keeps grazing animals out of one plot. Which plot keeps more kinds of plants, and why?
cards.back: The grazed plot. Grazing animals that eat enough plants let light back in, so more kinds of small plants survive.
cards.quote: Where grazing animals ate enough plants to let light back in, more kinds of plants survived.
cards.section: The grassland nutrient experiment

cards.front: In a greenhouse, a soybean that cannot form nodules had mean dry mass 12.37 g with no added nitrogen, 27.77 g at 50 mg per kg, 47.75 g at 100 mg and 32.40 g at 150 mg. Which dose gave the biggest plant, and what does 150 mg show?
cards.back: 100 mg per kg gave the biggest plant, 47.75 g. At 150 mg the mass fell to 32.40 g, so more fertilizer did not always give a bigger plant.
cards.quote: So more fertilizer did not always give a bigger plant.
cards.section: A greenhouse test of nitrogen dose

cards.front: A field has plenty of usable nitrogen but is shaded and dry. Will adding more nitrogen fertilizer raise growth much?
cards.back: Probably not. Usable nitrogen sets growth only where nitrogen runs short. Here light or water holds growth back instead.
cards.quote: And usable nitrogen sets growth only where nitrogen runs short; water, light or other nutrients can hold growth back instead.
